pos: n. (William Salesbury, c. 1520–c. 1584, translator of the first Welsh New Testament)
etymology: Germanic Wilhelm, resolute protector; English Salesbury, of Salisbury, a place-name surname.
biblical_def: William Salesbury was a Denbighshire gentleman, trained in the law at Oxford, who turned the whole of his learning on one object: the Welsh language as a vehicle for Scripture. He compiled the first Welsh-English dictionary, wrote on Welsh pronunciation and on the proverbs of the Welsh, and then with Bishop Richard Davies and Thomas Huet produced the Welsh New Testament and Prayer Book of 1567 under the Act of Parliament that required them. His translation is dense, archaic and full of deliberate Latinisms, and later Welshmen complained of its style; it was nonetheless the first time a Welsh-speaking congregation heard the gospels read in its own tongue from a printed book. The dictionary records the complaint and the achievement together. A first translation is almost always heavy, because the translator is making decisions nobody has made before and reaching for a dignity the language has not yet been given in print. Morgan's great Bible of 1588 stands on Salesbury's shoulders and says so.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines lexicographer as the author of a dictionary, and vernacular as native, of one's birth-country.
webster_full: LEXICOG'RAPHER, n. The author of a lexicon or dictionary.
VERNAC'ULAR, a. Native; belonging to the country of one's birth; as one's vernacular tongue.
ORTHOEP'Y, n. The art of uttering words with propriety; a correct pronunciation of words.
VER'SION, n. A translation; that which is rendered from another language.

corruption_summary: His 1567 New Testament was the first printed Welsh Scripture, heavy in style and foundational all the same.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is impatience with first attempts. Salesbury's Welsh was criticised almost at once for its Latinate orthography and its hard constructions, and the criticism was partly just; but the alternative to a heavy first translation is no translation, and the critics had a text to improve only because he made one.

The principle to recover is that hearing in one's own tongue is the ordinary means of faith, and that getting the text into the language comes before polishing it. “And how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?” (Act 2:8). Without intelligibility there is nothing: “for ye shall speak into the air” (1Co 14:9). The sense must be given so that hearers understand — “and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8) — because “faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Rom 10:17).

pos: n. (Richard Davies, c. 1501–1581, Marian exile and Bishop of St Davids, co-translator of the Welsh New Testament)
etymology: Germanic Ricohard, strong in rule; Welsh Davies, son of David.
biblical_def: Richard Davies went into exile at Frankfurt under Mary, returned at Elizabeth's accession, and was made Bishop of St Davids, where he gave himself to the Welsh Scriptures. He translated part of the 1567 New Testament, pressed the project through, and wrote the long Welsh preface to it, addressed to his countrymen, which argued that the Britons had received a pure apostolic Christianity long before Augustine of Canterbury came, that Rome had afterwards imposed on them, and that the Reformation was therefore a restoration of what the Welsh had once had. The dictionary quotes that argument with care. Its historical reconstruction is partly legend, and the dictionary does not pretend otherwise; but its theological instinct is exactly right, and it is the instinct of the whole Reformation: what is being recovered is older than what is being removed. Davies told the Welsh that Protestantism was not an English novelty imposed upon them, and on the substance he was correct.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines preface as an introduction to a discourse or book, and primitive as original, of the earliest age.
webster_full: PREF'ACE, n. Something spoken as introductory to a discourse, or written as introductory to a book.
PRIM'ITIVE, a. Pertaining to the beginning or origin; original; first; as the primitive church.
RESTORA'TION, n. The act of replacing in a former state; renewal; revival; re-establishment.
BISH'OP, n. An overseer; a spiritual superintendent, ruler or director.

corruption_summary: His Welsh preface of 1567 told his countrymen the Reformation restored what Britain had held before Rome came.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the charge, as old as the Reformation and still in use, that Protestantism is a sixteenth-century invention and therefore an innovation. Davies answered it on two levels. His historical level — an ancient British church independent of Rome — is embroidered. His doctrinal level is sound and sufficient on its own: the faith the Reformers preached is the faith delivered once to the saints, and the additions are what came later.

The principle to recover is that the old way is the test and the new teaching bears the burden of proof. “Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein” (Jer 6:16). The faith was delivered once: “earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3). It is tested against Scripture and not against pedigree — “searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11) — and any later gospel stands condemned: “If any man preach any other gospel unto you than that ye have received, let him be accursed” (Gal 1:9).

pos: n. (William Morgan, 1545–1604, translator of the complete Welsh Bible of 1588, Bishop of St Asaph)
etymology: Germanic Wilhelm, resolute protector; Welsh Morgan, sea-born or sea-chief.
biblical_def: William Morgan was a Caernarvonshire man, educated at Cambridge in Hebrew and Greek, and vicar of the remote parish of Llanrhaeadr-ym-Mochnant when he undertook to translate the whole Bible into Welsh. He worked from the Hebrew and the Greek, revising Salesbury's New Testament and rendering the entire Old Testament himself, and the book was printed in London in 1588 and sent to every parish church in Wales. He was afterwards Bishop of Llandaff and then of St Asaph. The dictionary gives his Bible the place it gave the Authorized Version in England and the Kralice Bible in Bohemia. Morgan's prose fixed literary Welsh for three centuries; it is the reason Welsh survived as a written and preached language when Cornish did not; and it put the whole counsel of God into the hands of a people most of whom had no English. One scholar in a hill parish, working at night, did more for Wales than any statute.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines translate as to render into another language, and standard as that which is established as a rule or model.
webster_full: TRANSLA'TE, v.t. To interpret; to render into another language; to express the sense of one language in the words of another.
STAND'ARD, n. That which is established by sovereign power as a rule or measure; a model.
PAR'ISH, n. The precinct or territorial jurisdiction of a secular priest, or the particular church which he serves.
ORIG'INAL, a. First in order; as the original languages of the Scriptures.

Isa 40:8

corruption_summary: His 1588 Bible from the Hebrew and Greek fixed literary Welsh and kept the language alive for three centuries.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern separation of the Bible's spiritual work from its cultural effects, as though the survival of the Welsh language were a happy accident unrelated to the preaching of the gospel in it. It was not an accident. A people that reads, memorises, preaches and sings in a tongue keeps the tongue, and the one book everybody in Wales had was Morgan's.

The principle to recover is that nothing of the counsel of God is to be withheld and nothing added to it. Paul could say “For I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God” (Act 20:27), and a whole Bible rather than a lectionary is how a church obeys that. The text is fixed: “Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought from it” (Deu 4:2). It outlasts the nations that print it — “but the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8) — and the publishing of it is a company's work: “great was the company of those that published it” (Psa 68:11).

pos: n. (Edmwnd Prys, 1543–1623, Archdeacon of Merioneth and author of the Welsh metrical Psalter)
etymology: Germanic Eadmund, blessed protection; Welsh Prys, from ap Rhys, son of Rhys.
biblical_def: Edmwnd Prys was Archdeacon of Merioneth, a poet of standing in the strict Welsh bardic metres, and the man who gave Wales its singing Psalter. His Salmau Can of 1621 put the hundred and fifty Psalms into simple Welsh metre with a handful of tunes, printed with the Prayer Book, and Welsh congregations sang them for three hundred years; a good many Welsh people of the nineteenth century knew the Psalter by heart in his words. He was a learned man who deliberately wrote plainly, setting aside the elaborate bardic craft he had mastered because a congregation cannot sing it. The dictionary honours that renunciation. A poet who can do the difficult thing and chooses the plain thing for the sake of people who cannot read has made a pastoral decision, and it is the same decision every translator and hymnwriter in this night's batches had to make.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines metre as the rhythmical arrangement of syllables into verses, and bard as a poet and singer among the ancient Celts.
webster_full: ME'TRE, n. Rhythmical arrangement of syllables or words into verses, stanzas, strophes.
BARD, n. A poet and a singer among the ancient Celts; one whose occupation was to compose and sing verses.
PSAL'TER, n. The Book of Psalms; a psalm-book.
ARCHDE'ACON, n. An ecclesiastical dignitary next in rank below a bishop.

corruption_summary: A master of the bardic metres who wrote plainly so that Welsh congregations could sing the Psalms.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the use of skill to exclude. A musician or poet of real ability can write congregational song that only the able can sing, and call the result excellence; Prys had the ability and spent it on simplicity, which is the harder discipline and the more useful.

The principle to recover is that public worship is measured by what edifies the congregation. Paul had rather “speak five words with my understanding, that by my voice I might teach others also, than ten thousand words in an unknown tongue” (1Co 14:19) — which is a judgment about intelligibility, not about effort. The Psalms are to be taught and sung together: “teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (Col 3:16). And the command is addressed to the whole assembly — “Sing unto the LORD a new song, and his praise in the congregation of saints” (Psa 149:1).

pos: n. (John Davies of Mallwyd, c. 1567–1644, Welsh grammarian and chief hand in the 1620 revision of the Welsh Bible)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan through Latin Johannes, the LORD is gracious; Welsh Davies, son of David; Mallwyd, a Merioneth parish.
biblical_def: John Davies was rector of Mallwyd in Merioneth for more than forty years and the finest Welsh philologist of his age. He published a grammar of Welsh and a Welsh-Latin dictionary which remained standard into the nineteenth century, and he was the principal working hand in the revision of Morgan's Bible issued in 1620 under Bishop Richard Parry — the text that became, in effect, the Welsh Authorized Version and the form in which Welsh people read the Scriptures until modern times. He also rebuilt his church and its bridges at his own charge. The dictionary names him for the revision. A translation is a living thing that needs correction, and the man who performs that correction is giving up the credit of authorship for the good of the text; Parry's name went on the title page and Davies did the work. The best translating has very often been done by the second man.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines revision as the act of reviewing and correcting, and grammarian as one versed in the construction of language.
webster_full: REVI'SION, n. The act of reviewing; review; re-examination for correction.
GRAMMA'RIAN, n. One versed in grammar; one who teaches grammar.
REC'TOR, n. A clergyman who has the charge and cure of a parish, and receives the tithes.
PHILOL'OGY, n. That branch of literature which comprehends a knowledge of the etymology and construction of words.

corruption_summary: He did the work of the 1620 Welsh Bible revision while another man's name went on the title page.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the appetite for credit, which makes revision an unattractive calling: nobody is remembered for improving another man's book. Davies spent years on Morgan's text, improving the renderings and regularising the orthography, and what Wales read for three centuries was his version of Morgan's work under Parry's name.

The principle to recover is that exactness in handling Scripture is itself worship, and that the right word is worth the labour. “rightly dividing the word of truth” (2Ti 2:15). The fitting word is praised in Proverbs: “A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver” (Pro 25:11). The Preacher sought such words and wrote them down uprightly — “The preacher sought to find out acceptable words: and that which was written was upright, even words of truth” (Ecc 12:10) — and the end is always that the hearers understand: “caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8).

pos: n. (Rhys Prichard, c. 1579–1644, Vicar of Llandovery, author of The Welshman's Candle)
etymology: Welsh Rhys, ardour, a rush; Prichard, from ap Richard, son of Richard.
biblical_def: Rhys Prichard, remembered simply as the Vicar of Llandovery, spent his ministry in Carmarthenshire writing short Welsh verses on the plainest matters of the faith — the ten commandments, the Lord's Prayer, the sabbath, drunkenness, death, the cross — in the simplest possible metre, four-line stanzas a labourer could memorise after hearing them twice. They circulated by voice and in manuscript during his lifetime and were printed after his death as Cannwyll y Cymry, the Welshman's Candle, which became for two centuries the most read book in Wales after the Bible. The dictionary honours the deliberate plainness. Prichard was an Oxford man preaching to a population with very little literacy, and he judged that what they would retain was verse. He was right; Welsh people who could not read recited his stanzas on their deathbeds, and the Methodist revival of the next century broke out among people whose doctrine he had largely formed.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines candle as a light formed of tallow or wax, and catechise as to instruct by question and answer.
webster_full: CAN'DLE, n. A long but small cylindrical body of tallow, wax or spermaceti, containing a wick and used for a portable light.
CAT'ECHISE, v.t. To instruct by asking questions and receiving answers, and by correcting the answers.
STAN'ZA, n. In poetry, a number of lines or verses connected with each other.
VIC'AR, n. The incumbent of an appropriated or impropriated ecclesiastical living.

corruption_summary: His four-line Welsh stanzas became the most read book in Wales after the Bible.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a snobbery about simplicity that runs in both directions: the educated preacher who will not stoop to a four-line stanza, and the populariser who stoops and leaves the doctrine behind. Prichard's verses are simple in form and entirely doctrinal in content; they teach law, sin, atonement, sabbath and judgment, in words a child could carry.

The principle to recover is that God Himself teaches by repetition in small portions. “For precept must be upon precept, precept upon precept; line upon line, line upon line; here a little, and there a little” (Isa 28:10). The commandment is itself the light the title borrowed: “For the commandment is a lamp; and the law is light” (Pro 6:23). Such a light is not to be hidden — “Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel” (Mat 5:15) — and the household is the first schoolroom: “And ye shall teach them your children” (Deu 11:19).

pos: n. (Walter Cradock, c. 1606–1659, Welsh Puritan preacher and founder with Wroth of the church at Llanvaches)
etymology: Germanic Waldhari, ruler of the army; Welsh Cradock, from Caradog, beloved.
biblical_def: Walter Cradock was silenced as a curate at Cardiff for his preaching, took to itinerating through Monmouthshire and the Welsh border, and in 1639 helped gather at Llanvaches the first Independent church in Wales, on the pattern of the New England congregations. He preached through the civil war, was one of the approved itinerants for Wales under the Commonwealth, and died shortly before the Restoration which would have ejected him. Unusually for his party he was known for charity toward those who differed with him, and he said in a sermon before Parliament that he had rather see men preaching the gospel with errors in their judgment than see them silenced. The dictionary records both the gathering of the church and the temper. Cradock belonged to the generation that made Wales Nonconformist, and the Welsh chapels of the next two centuries trace to the handful of congregations he and Wroth and their fellows gathered in the border counties.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines itinerate as to travel from place to place, particularly to preach, and congregation as an assembly met for worship.
webster_full: ITIN'ERATE, v.i. To travel from place to place, particularly for the purpose of preaching.
CONGREGA'TION, n. An assembly of persons met for the worship of God.
SI'LENCE, v.t. To put to silence; to restrain from preaching by revoking a license.
INDEPEND'ENT, n. One who holds that each congregation of Christians is a complete church, subject to no external authority.

corruption_summary: Silenced at Cardiff, he itinerated and helped gather the first Independent church in Wales in 1639.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the party spirit that measures a man's soundness by his willingness to silence his neighbours. Cradock held definite convictions and gathered a church on them; he also judged that a preached gospel with some error in it does more good than an enforced silence, which is a distinction worth keeping and is easily abused in either direction.

The principle to recover is that the gospel is to be preached as the preachers go, and that God uses imperfect preachers. The commission is given on the road: “And as ye go, preach, saying, The kingdom of heaven is at hand” (Mat 10:7). The Lord sent out seventy more besides the twelve, “two and two before his face into every city and place” (Luk 10:1). Scattering produced preaching: “they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word” (Act 8:4). And Paul's own judgment, about men whose motives were worse than their doctrine, was “Christ is preached; and I therein do rejoice” (Phi 1:18).

pos: n. (Morgan Llwyd, 1619–1659, Welsh Puritan preacher and author of The Book of the Three Birds)
biblical_def: Morgan Llwyd was converted under Cradock's preaching, served as a chaplain in the parliamentary armies, and settled at Wrexham, where he wrote the Welsh prose for which he is remembered. Llyfr y Tri Aderyn, the Book of the Three Birds, is a dialogue between an eagle, a dove and a raven on the state of the nation and the soul, and it is reckoned among the finest things written in Welsh prose. Llwyd also held strongly millenarian expectations, was for a time drawn toward the Fifth Monarchy men, and read Jacob Boehme with sympathy. The dictionary names the gift and the error without blending them. The prose is a glory of the Welsh language and the inward illuminism and the date-setting are not; a Christian may write beautifully about the soul and still be wrong about the times, and the Scripture that corrects him is the plainest in the New Testament on the subject.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines millenarian as one who believes in the millennium, and allegory as a figurative discourse in which the principal subject is described by another.
webster_full: MILLENA'RIAN, n. One who believes in the millennium, and that it will shortly appear.
AL'LEGORY, n. A figurative sentence or discourse, in which the principal subject is described by another subject resembling it.
ILLUMINA'TION, n. Infusion of intellectual light; inspiration; a pretended inward light.

corruption_summary: A master of Welsh prose whose millenarian date-setting and inward illuminism the dictionary names as error.
corruption_paragraphs: The errors to name are two and they travel together. The first is the setting of dates for Christ's kingdom, which in the 1650s drove the Fifth Monarchy movement and has recurred in every century since with the same result. The second is illuminism, the expectation of an inward light that discloses what Scripture does not, which Llwyd found in Boehme and which always ends by making the reader's experience the authority. Neither error is harmless and neither is cured by the beauty of the prose that carries it.

The standard is our Lord's own refusal to give the information. “It is not for you to know the times or the seasons, which the Father hath put in his own power” (Act 1:7). “But of that day and hour knoweth no man, no, not the angels of heaven, but my Father only” (Mat 24:36). The manner of the coming forbids calculation: “the day of the Lord so cometh as a thief in the night” (1Th 5:2). And every claimed illumination is to be tried by the written word — “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20).

pos: n. (Vavasor Powell, 1617–1670, Welsh Puritan itinerant and Baptist, who died in prison)
etymology: Old French vavassour, a vassal's vassal, used as a given name; Welsh Powell, from ap Hywel, son of Hywel.
biblical_def: Vavasor Powell was the most tireless itinerant preacher Wales produced in that century. Converted in his twenties, he rode the Welsh counties preaching in houses, fields and market places, gathered congregations, came to Baptist convictions on baptism, and quarrelled publicly with Cromwell over the Protectorate. After the Restoration he was arrested again and again, spent most of the last decade of his life in gaol, and died in the Fleet prison in London in 1670, having been offered release on terms he would not take. The dictionary records the count: he was imprisoned in eight or nine different places across eleven years. Powell is the plainest Welsh instance of a man who could have been quiet and was not, and whose congregations — meeting illegally in barns and on hillsides through the persecuting years — became the Welsh Baptist and Independent churches of the eighteenth century.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines conventicle as a secret or unlawful assembly for religious worship, and persevere as to persist in any business.
webster_full: CONVEN'TICLE, n. An assembly for religious worship; appropriately, a secret or unlawful assembly.
PERSEVE'RE, v.i. To persist in any business or enterprise undertaken; to pursue steadily any design.
GA'OL, n. A prison; a place for the confinement of debtors and criminals.
ITIN'ERANT, a. Passing or travelling about the country; wandering; not settled.

corruption_summary: Imprisoned in eight or nine gaols across eleven years, he refused release on terms and died in the Fleet.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern assumption that a man in that position should have taken the terms. Powell was repeatedly offered liberty on condition of giving bond not to preach, and he would not; the calculation that one may buy freedom by promising silence looks prudent and surrenders the thing the imprisonment was about.

The principle to recover is that the command to preach is not the magistrate's to revoke. “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29). The bonds do not reach the word: “I suffer trouble, as an evil doer, even unto bonds; but the word of God is not bound” (2Ti 2:9). The eleventh of Hebrews lists his lot exactly — “yea, moreover of bonds and imprisonment” (Heb 11:36) — and the promise for a man who dies in a gaol is specific: “be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life” (Rev 2:10).

pos: n. (Stephen Hughes, 1622–1688, ejected Welsh minister, printer of Welsh Bibles and books)
etymology: Greek Stephanos, a crown; Welsh Hughes, son of Hugh.
biblical_def: Stephen Hughes was vicar of Meidrim in Carmarthenshire until the Act of Uniformity put him out in 1662, and he spent the remaining twenty-six years of his life getting Welsh books into Welsh hands. He collected and printed the verses of Rhys Prichard, saw editions of the Welsh Bible and New Testament through the London presses, published Welsh catechisms and a Welsh version of the first part of Pilgrim's Progress, and funded much of it by subscription from sympathetic gentry and merchants. He was called the Apostle of Carmarthenshire. The dictionary names him as the model of what an ejected minister may do when the pulpit is closed. Hughes could not preach legally; he could print, and he judged that a Bible in a farmhouse outlasts a sermon. The Welsh revival of the following century ran through districts saturated with the books he distributed, and he had been dead fifty years when it came.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines eject as to throw out and dispossess, and subscription as a sum subscribed toward a book or undertaking.
webster_full: EJECT', v.t. To throw out; to cast forth; to dispossess of an office or benefice.
SUBSCRIP'TION, n. A paper to which names are subscribed; the sum subscribed toward the publication of a book.
DISTRIB'UTE, v.t. To divide among two or more; to deal out; to bestow in parts.
APOS'TLE, n. A person deputed to execute some important business; one of the twelve disciples of Christ.

corruption_summary: Ejected in 1662, he spent twenty-six years printing Welsh Bibles and books instead of preaching.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the assumption that a silenced minister's usefulness is over. Hughes lost the one thing he had been trained for and immediately found the second-best thing and did it for a quarter of a century, with results he never saw. Nonconformity in Wales was built far more on his distributed books than on any surviving pulpit.

The principle to recover is that the word is to be written and scattered, and that the sowing and the reaping are not in the same hand. “Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables” (Hab 2:2). “Cast thy bread upon the waters: for thou shalt find it after many days” (Ecc 11:1). The sowing is to continue without knowing which part will take: “In the morning sow thy seed, and in the evening withhold not thine hand” (Ecc 11:6). And the promise to the man who sows weeping is kept, often long after him — “He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him” (Psa 126:6).
